answer.benchmark_name: MasakhaNER (Twi test set, original MasakhaNER 1.0 BIO tagging)
answer.known_results: MasakhaNER is a named entity recognition dataset for African languages (Adelani et al., 2021), with PER, ORG, LOC and DATE tags. Fine-tuned models such as AfroXLMR and mT5 reach about 80–90 F1 on many languages. Twi is one of the harder ones, with F1 in the 60s–70s. Zero-shot LLM prompting generally scores lower than fine-tuned models.

The items look like MMLU-style multiple-choice questions (marketing, elementary math, clinical nutrition/medical genetics), but I can't say for sure which benchmark they come from. I'm not naming one.

answer.benchmark_name: Exercism-based coding benchmark (e.g., Aider Polyglot, which uses Exercism exercises in C++ and other languages)
answer.known_results: The items are Exercism exercises (spiral-matrix, classification of numbers, binary search tree) with C++ starter files. This matches the Aider Polyglot benchmark, which has 225 hard Exercism problems across 6 languages. Frontier models score roughly 60-90% on it, depending on the model and the edit format used. I'm not certain it is Polyglot and not a similar Exercism-derived set.

answer.benchmark_name: BIRD (BIg Bench for LaRge-scale Database Grounded Text-to-SQL Evaluation)
answer.known_results: The BIRD dev set has databases such as superhero, california_schools and codebase_community. Execution accuracy is the main metric. Human performance is about 92.96%. Early GPT-4 results were about 54%, and later specialized systems reach roughly 70-75% on the dev or test set.

BBQ (Parrish et al., 2022) tests social bias with ambiguous and disambiguated contexts. Models usually score high on disambiguated items. They score lower on ambiguous items, where they tend to follow stereotypes instead of choosing "unknown". These items are all disambiguated, so strong modern models get them almost all correct (above 90%).

answer.benchmark_name: BIRD (BIg Bench for LaRge-scale Database Grounded Text-to-SQL Evaluation), dev set
answer.known_results: The BIRD dev set has 1,534 questions. Execution accuracy was about 50-60% for early LLM baselines such as ChatGPT. Top systems with GPT-4 or o1-class models and agentic pipelines reach about 70-76% on dev. Human performance is about 92.96%.

Belebele is Meta's multilingual reading comprehension benchmark covering 122 language variants. Large LLMs score high on English, but low-resource languages like Northern Sotho score much lower. Top models such as GPT-4 reach roughly 50–80% on these languages, and smaller models score near chance (25%). I don't recall exact figures for this language.

answer.benchmark_name: scEval / cell type annotation from ranked gene lists (multiple sclerosis snRNA-seq, Schirmer et al. 2019 data), e.g., C2S-style or "LLM cell type annotation" benchmark
answer.known_results: I don't recall exact scores. General-purpose LLMs like GPT-4 do reasonably well on such gene-ranking cell type annotation tasks, with moderate accuracy, while fine-tuned models usually do better.

answer.benchmark_name: MATH (Hendrycks et al.) / MATH-500, as used in Llama 3.1 evaluation format
answer.known_results: The problems look like MATH dataset items (Algebra, Number Theory, Geometry), probably from the MATH-500 subset. Frontier models now score above 90% on MATH-500. Llama 3.1 405B scored about 73.8% on MATH with 0-shot CoT.

C-Eval is a Chinese multi-discipline multiple-choice benchmark with 52 subjects. It uses subjects such as elementary Chinese, Chinese history, and law and moral foundations. I recall that GPT-4 scored about 68.7% at launch, and recent top models score above 90%. I'm not sure the items are from C-Eval rather than a similar benchmark such as CMMLU.

answer.benchmark_name: CRUXEval (CRUXEval-I input prediction and CRUXEval-O output prediction)
answer.known_results: CRUXEval (Gu et al., 2024, Meta) has 800 Python functions. Items 1 and 2 are input prediction (CRUXEval-I). Item 3 is output prediction (CRUXEval-O). At release, GPT-4 with chain of thought scored about 75% on CRUXEval-I and 81% on CRUXEval-O. Open code models such as CodeLlama scored much lower, around 40-50%. Newer frontier models score higher, often above 90%.

DevBench compares vision-language models with child/adult human response patterns on developmentally inspired tasks, including lexical (vocabulary) and grammar (TROG) tasks. Models perform reasonably but don't fully match humans' response distributions. I don't remember precise numbers.

answer.benchmark_name: Ego4D (Goal-Step / Narrations; egocentric video narrations, possibly EgoSchema-derived)
answer.known_results: The "#C C ..." narration format with "#O" for other people comes from Ego4D. 180-second clips suggest a benchmark built on Ego4D narrations, such as EgoSchema. I don't recall specific scores. I think models score well below humans, who get about 76% on EgoSchema.

I only recall the name from the file paths (EDU-CIRCUIT-HW_v1). It is a dataset of handwritten circuit-analysis homework solutions from university students. I don't remember specific scores for AI systems.

These items look like BIG-Bench Hard subtasks (web of lies, causal judgment, object counting). Scores vary by task. Early models like PaLM were below the average human rater. Chain-of-thought prompting raised them a lot, and recent frontier models score about 90% or higher on average.

FinanceBench (Patronus AI, 2023) has 10,231 questions on public company filings. GPT-4-Turbo with a retrieval system answered only about 50% correctly, and many were refused or wrong. Long-context and oracle-context setups did better, and newer models score much higher.

HallusionBench tests image-context reasoning with yes/no questions, split into Visual Dependent (VD) and Visual Supplement (VS) categories. GPT-4V scored about 65% question-level accuracy and about 31% on paired-question accuracy at release. Open-source models scored lower, and even later frontier models stayed well below human performance.

answer.benchmark_name: IrokoBench-like African-language MMLU/Winogrande translations (likely Uhura or "AfroBench"/Winogrande-ZA/MMLU-Clinical-ZA style)
answer.known_results: I don't recall specific scores. Low-resource African languages like Tsonga and Bambara generally see markedly lower accuracy than English, often near chance for smaller models.

BBQ (Parrish et al., 2022) tests social bias in QA with ambiguous and disambiguated contexts. Models score high on disambiguated items, often above 90% for modern LLMs. They do worse on ambiguous items, where they tend to pick stereotyped answers instead of "unknown", though recent frontier models score much better.

answer.benchmark_name: IgakuQA (Japanese National Medical Licensing Examination QA)
answer.known_results: These look like questions from the Japanese national medical licensing exam (医師国家試験), as in IgakuQA or similar datasets. GPT-4 scored about 75–80% and passed. Later models scored above 90%. I'm not sure which exact dataset these items come from.

The items look like LegalBench tasks: the rhetorical-function classification of court opinion paragraphs (Facts, Issue, Rule, Analysis, Conclusion, Decree) and the GLOBALCIT citizenship-law yes/no questions. I don't remember exact scores. Frontier LLMs generally score about 70-85% on average across its 162 tasks, with wide variation between tasks.

answer.benchmark_name: MiniF2F (Lean 4 version, as used in DeepSeek-Prover / Kimina-Prover formatting)
answer.known_results: The problems are from the MiniF2F benchmark (244 valid and 244 test problems). Specialized provers score highly: DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5 about 50-63%, and DeepSeek-Prover-V2 671B about 88.9% on the test set. Kimina-Prover and Goedel-Prover-V2 score in the 80s to 90s.
These look like geometry problems from Geometry3K-style data. That data appears in MathVista and similar collections, but I can't tell which benchmark these items come from.

PubMedQA (Jin et al., 2019) has yes/no/maybe questions from PubMed abstracts. Single human annotators reach about 78% accuracy. Fine-tuned biomedical models scored about 70–80%, and recent large LLMs score about 75–82%.
Introduced by Hendrycks et al. (2020). GPT-3 scored about 44% and human experts about 90%. Frontier models now score around 88–93%, so the benchmark is largely saturated.
MMLU-Pro has 10 answer options per question, drawn from MMLU and other sources like STEM exam sets. Frontier models score roughly 70-90%, and older models like GPT-4 scored about 70% or lower.

answer.benchmark_name: MATH (Minerva 4-shot prompt, e.g. MATH / MATH-500 / Hendrycks MATH)
answer.known_results: The items are the Minerva 4-shot prompt exemplars, which are used to evaluate on the MATH dataset (Hendrycks et al.). Early models scored under 10%. Frontier reasoning models now score over 95% on MATH-500.

answer.benchmark_name: HANCOCK (Head and Neck Cancer Multimodal Dataset, Erlangen/Hancock cohort) – multimodal case-based benchmark
answer.known_results: I recognize the HANCOCK multimodal head and neck squamous cell carcinoma dataset (H&E, TMA IHC for CD3/CD8/CD56/CD68/CD163, clinical data). I don't recall specific AI scores on this agentic or case-based evaluation built from it.

The items are Django Trac issues, which matches SWE-bench's Django subset. I don't recall exact scores for this subset. On SWE-bench Verified, frontier models have scored roughly 70-80% or more, and Django is one of the larger repositories in the set.

answer.benchmark_name: NYU CTF Bench (NYU CTF Dataset, CSAW CTF challenges)
answer.known_results: The benchmark is built from CSAW CTF qualifier and final challenges (2017–2023). I recall that LLM agents solve only a small share of it. Reported results were roughly 5–10% for the best models, such as GPT-4 and Claude 3.5 Sonnet, with many categories near zero. I don't remember exact figures.
These look like indirect object identification (IOI) templates from the interpretability work on GPT-2 small (Wang et al.). I can't tie them to a specific named benchmark with published scores.

Theorem names like mathd_algebra_342 and algebra_sqineq_at2malt1 are from MiniF2F. Early LLM provers, such as Thor and Draft-Sketch-Prove, solved roughly 30–45% of the test set. Recent systems report much higher rates, with some above 60–90% on Isabelle or Lean variants.

In PlanBench (Valmeekam et al.), the obfuscated Mystery Blocksworld was very hard for LLMs: GPT-4 solved only a few percent. Reasoning models like o1 do much better but still fail on many instances, especially the longer ones.

Not recognized. The items look like graduate-level multiple-choice science questions (physics, molecular biology, organic chemistry) in the style of GPQA or a similar set. I can't identify the specific benchmark with confidence.

I'm not certain of the exact benchmark. The items are GitHub issues from Java repos (RocketMQ, Dubbo, Gson), which fits Multi-SWE-bench's Java subset. As I recall, resolve rates there are much lower than on SWE-bench Verified, usually well under 30% for Java.

From memory: in the original τ-bench paper, GPT-4o scored about 35% pass^1 on the airline domain. Later models score higher (Claude 3.7 Sonnet around 58%, newer Claude models around 70% or more). Pass^k drops sharply as k increases.

answer.benchmark_name: τ²-bench (tau-squared bench), with retail and telecom domains
answer.known_results: I recall that τ-bench (Sierra) introduced the retail and airline domains. τ²-bench added the telecom domain, where the user also acts on the device. Telecom is generally the hardest domain for models. Frontier models score well on retail, roughly 70–85% pass^1, and their telecom scores vary widely. I can't give exact figures.

answer.benchmark_name: TruthfulQA (multiple-choice, MC1/MC2 with the default QA prompt)
answer.known_results: Introduced by Lin et al. (2021). The best model at the time, GPT-3 175B, was truthful on about 58% of questions, against 94% for humans. Larger models often did worse (inverse scaling). Later instruction-tuned and RLHF models score much higher, around 60-80%+ on MC tasks.

I recall this as a large collection of about 1,600 instruction-defined NLP tasks, used for instruction-tuning and evaluation. Scores are usually ROUGE-L. Tk-Instruct (11B) got about 62% ROUGE-L on held-out tasks, ahead of InstructGPT and other baselines of that period. I'm not certain these three items come from it, since the prompts could also come from a related instruction dataset.

MedCalc-Bench (Khandekar et al., 2024) tests LLMs on computing medical values from patient notes. Models did poorly at first: GPT-4 scored about 50% with one-shot prompting, and open-source models scored lower. Later reasoning models score much higher.

WorkArena++ is a ServiceNow benchmark of compositional, long-horizon enterprise workflow tasks, including change request scheduling and list sorting. Agents score low. GPT-4o-based agents solve only a few percent of tasks, and humans score much higher. I don't remember exact figures.

WorkBench (Styles et al., 2024) is a workplace-simulation benchmark with five databases (email, calendar, web analytics, CRM, project management) and 26 tools. I recall GPT-4 scoring about 43% and weaker open models such as Llama2-70B scoring very low, around 3%. Many failures came from wrong or unintended side-effect actions.

answer.benchmark_name: SWE-bench Multimodal / multi-language GitHub issue resolution (SWE-Gym or SWE-bench-extra style, e.g., nemotron/SWE-rebench)
answer.known_results: Not sure of the exact benchmark. The items look like GitHub issues from Python repos (darker, zope.schema, dvc), which fits SWE-Gym or SWE-rebench style datasets. Top agents resolve roughly 50-70% on SWE-bench Verified, and I can't give a specific score for this one.

AppWorld tasks use simulated apps (Amazon, Spotify, SimpleNote, Gmail) with API-based agents. Frontier LLM agents scored low at launch (GPT-4o about 49% on test-normal, about 30% on test-challenge). Newer agents have scored much higher.

answer.benchmark_name: MEDEC (MEDEC: A Benchmark for Medical Error Detection and Correction in Clinical Notes)
answer.known_results: MEDEC (Microsoft/UW, 2024) has clinical notes from MedQA-derived and MS/UW sources, with error detection, sentence ID extraction and correction tasks. LLMs like GPT-4, Claude 3.5 Sonnet and o1-preview score well below physicians on error detection and correction. Claude 3.5 Sonnet did relatively well at detection and o1-preview was best overall.

KernelBench (Stanford, Ouyang et al. 2025) tasks LLMs with writing fast CUDA kernels to replace PyTorch Model modules. Frontier models produce correct and faster kernels (fast_1) on only a minority of tasks, especially at Level 1. Reasoning models like o1 and DeepSeek-R1 did best, and results improve with iterative refinement and execution feedback.

BABILong embeds bAbI task facts (qa1–qa20) in long PG19 distractor text. LLMs do well at short contexts, but accuracy falls sharply as length grows. Models often use only 10–20% of their stated context window effectively. RAG and fine-tuned recurrent-memory models do better on some tasks.

AlgoTune (2025) asks LMs to write code that runs faster than reference solvers (scipy, cvxpy, etc.) across about 150 tasks. It scores by average speedup over the reference, and the best models, such as o4-mini and DeepSeek R1, reached only about 1.5–2x average speedup. I'm not certain of the exact figures.
